prize_parts.citation: For showing how productivity differences across firms and selection into exporting and foreign investment shape trade patterns, resource reallocation and the gains from trade.

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: one part, B014, crediting Melitz and Helpman. I have tightened the citation to selection, reallocation and firm-level sorting into exporting and FDI. It no longer makes any claim about the size of aggregate welfare gains. The case rests on a single, well-bounded discovery. Trade analysis moved from representative firms to productivity-sorted firms, and that produced testable predictions that firm-level data then largely supported. The framework is more than twenty years old and is now a workhorse in trade, macroeconomics, IO and firm dynamics, so maturity is not in question. My own research on firm dynamics and creative destruction uses the same kind of firm-selection logic, which is part of why I see how widely it travels, and I disclose that below. I reread the B009 arguments carefully. B009 is mature, its identification is credible, and several colleagues have moved to it for substantive reasons. I still keep it as my first alternative, not my preferred part. The reason is that the committee has not yet decided what the B009 discovery is: the combined technology-and-trade account of labour demand (Autor, Hanson, Katz) or the China-shock evidence (Autor, Dorn, Hanson). Each choice leaves out a name that has a strong claim. I do not treat the split in explicit support for B009 as evidence of merit, either for or against it.
statement.case_against: The hardest point against B014 is priority. Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum (2003) built a heterogeneous-firm trade model at the same time as Melitz, and that line plus Bernard-Jensen's exporter-premium evidence is not credited here. Hopenhayn's firm-dynamics framework also underlies Melitz's setup. I said in round 1 that the models are distinct, and I still think the differences are real: monopolistic competition, fixed costs, free entry, and a tractable general-equilibrium treatment that transferred easily to other fields. But that is a judgement about which contribution carried further, not a proof of priority. Krugman's 2008 prize and Helpman's separate B049 candidacy are lesser concerns. The Arkolakis-Costinot-Rodriguez-Clare result shows that the size of the welfare gains from selection depends on functional-form assumptions. That is why I removed any claim about the size of the gains from the citation. A smaller, less sure point is that excluding Redding drops the quantitative and spatial extensions. I think those are consolidation of the core, not a separate discovery, but a committee member could see it differently.

responses.point: Dreber Almenberg ranks B014 sixth and asked me directly how I weigh Krugman 2008, the uncredited priority claims and the contested size of the welfare gains against the framework's reach. She treats those points as weightier than I seemed to.
responses.response: I rank the three concerns differently. Krugman 2008 weighs least with me. That prize concerned scale economies, product differentiation and trade patterns with representative firms, and firm selection is a different object. The welfare-gain critique mainly affects wording. The citation should say selection and reallocation and should not claim large gains, and I have rewritten it that way. Priority is the point that could move my ranking. A citation limited to selection and reallocation only partly resolves it, because Bernard-Eaton-Jensen-Kortum also generate selection and reallocation in a Ricardian setting. What favours the Melitz-Helpman credit is tractability, endogenous entry and the Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple link between exporting and FDI, which together made the framework usable across fields. I accept that this is a close and contestable call and not a clear win. It is also why I no longer say the gap between B014 and B009 is large.

responses.point: Teorell ranks B009 first with Autor, Hanson and Dorn on the China-shock strand. In round 1 he said he found B014 more persuasive after Friberg's argument and listed it as an alternative. He noted that the 2008 prize concerned trade patterns, not firm selection.
responses.response: I agree with his reading of Krugman 2008, and I take it as a sign that the B014 credit is more compact than the B009 credit. I also agree that the Dorn-or-Katz choice follows from how the discovery is defined. The chair asked what would lead me to prefer B009. The answer is a committee that first states one object, for example labour-market adjustment to technology and trade, and then names a trio that fits it. If the object were the trade shock alone, I would find his trio the most accurate. If the object were the wider account of wage structure, I would find Autor, Hanson and Katz, which I proposed in my opening, the most accurate. Under either definition I would regard B009 as a prize-worthy outcome. Where we differ is that I find B014's single-framework attribution firmer today. I do not claim more than that.

responses.point: Krusell ranks B009 first and keeps Autor, Katz and Hanson to span technology and trade. He ranks B014 fourth because of Krugman 2008 and the uncredited priority claims of Bernard, Eaton and Kortum.
responses.response: His priority point is the same one I accept as my main weakness, so we agree on the facts. We differ on how to weigh them. B009's mature wage-structure evidence deserves its weight. But his citation still joins two strands, one of which (the China-shock designs) is debated for persistence and shift-share inference. Within the three-name cap he must drop Dorn, who has an equal claim on that strand. B014's priority problem is real, but it involves adjacent models that arrived at the same time. B009's problem lies inside the credited object. I find that harder to fix with citation wording, though I do not think it is clearly worse in scientific merit.

responses.point: Friberg ranks B014 first with the cleanest pair, Melitz and Helpman, leaves out Redding, and says he cannot settle the Bernard-Jensen and Eaton-Kortum priority question from the supplied evidence.
responses.response: I agree on the pair and on leaving out Redding, whose quantitative and spatial work follows the core discovery. On priority, I share his stated limit. The discussion has not produced new evidence that decides it, and I would not claim it has. I do not think support for B014 should be argued from the gap since 2008. If the committee finds the priority claims too strong for a two-name citation, that is a legitimate reason to prefer B009, and I would not treat it as a failure of the B014 case. I only ask that the committee decide it explicitly. The wording should not hide an unresolved priority claim.

uncertainties: Whether Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum, and Hopenhayn's firm-dynamics framework, have claims strong enough that a Melitz-Helpman citation overstates novelty. The supplied evidence does not settle this.
Whether a citation limited to selection and reallocation is enough to answer the priority issue, or whether it only narrows what is claimed.
How much of the welfare-gain argument survives the Arkolakis-Costinot-Rodriguez-Clare critique, and whether that affects prize-level importance or only the wording.
For B009, whether the committee defines one discovery or two, and so whether Katz or Dorn belongs under the three-name cap. I would accept either coherent answer as a reason to move toward B009.
How Helpman's separate B049 candidacy should be handled in framing and credit. I would not want one prize to carry both rationales.
statement.conflict_note: Updated disclosure, unchanged in substance. The supplied profile documents a long-running collaboration with Peter Klenow, who is credited in B031, which I keep as an alternative. I disclose this and do not adjudicate it, and B031 is not my preferred part. Per Krusell (a frequent co-author) and John Hassler (a co-author) are IIES colleagues. Neither is a credited name on B014 or B009. My research on firm dynamics, creative destruction and structural change is adjacent to the heterogeneous-firm framework of B014. This is a field proximity, not a personal tie. The profile shows no collaboration with or institutional tie to Melitz, Helpman, Redding, Autor, Hanson, Katz or Dorn. The profile also notes that I co-authored popular summaries of the 2024 and 2025 prizes and that a rotated stamp on the 2025 Scientific Background may suggest drafting involvement. Neither bears on any shortlisted candidate. Everything here relies on the supplied profile and the round-1 files, and I claim no independent verification.
